content:
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟰 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱

An agent burns tokens, declares the task complete, and then fails the tests. That is often an architecture problem, not a prompting problem.

When an agent underperforms, the usual reflex is to rewrite the prompt or switch to a stronger model. But many failures actually come from the system around the model, and different problems need to be solved at different layers.

𝟭. 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽: repeats until evidence says stop

The loop is the smallest unit of agency. The agent acts, checks the result, and either stops or tries again.

The important part is how completion is decided. A reliable agent should not stop simply because the model believes the work looks correct. It should stop when there is external evidence, such as a passing test, a successful build, a validated output or another measurable condition.

Without this verification loop, an agent can confidently declare success while the task is still incomplete.

𝟮. 𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵: decides what runs next

A loop decides whether execution should continue. A graph decides where execution should go next.

It defines branches, retries, specialist-agent handoffs, fallback paths and shared state. Once a workflow has multiple possible routes, the graph makes those routes explicit, inspectable and controllable.

This is what turns repeated execution into a structured agent workflow.

𝟯. 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀: gives the model an operating environment

The model provides reasoning, but the harness determines what that reasoning can actually do.

It defines the tools, APIs, files, memory, permissions, context, logging and execution environment available to the model.

That distinction matters because model capability and agent capability are not the same thing. A model may understand exactly how to solve a task, but if the required tool, data source or permission is not exposed through the harness, the agent still cannot complete it.

A better prompt cannot compensate for a missing capability.

𝟰. 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗮-𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀: governs multiple agent harnesses

This layer becomes important when teams are using Claude Code, Codex, internal agents and specialised domain agents together.

Each may have its own tools, sessions, policies, permissions and execution environment. A meta-harness creates a common layer across them for orchestration, governance, isolation, shared policies and movement of context or workflows between different agents.

Omnigent is one open-source implementation of this layer, designed to provide a governed environment across different agent harnesses.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲:

Loop makes the work verifiable.
Graph makes the workflow structured.
Harness makes the model operational.
Meta-harness makes multiple agent environments governable.
A stronger model can improve reasoning, but reliable agents depend just as much on the architecture built around the model.

title:
Massive breakthrough here!

Researchers built a new AI inference engine that:

- reduces self-hosting costs by ~4x
- runs a full agentic pipeline on one GPU
- serves 20+ architectures, not just LLMs
content:
Massive breakthrough here!

Researchers built a new AI inference engine that:

- reduces self-hosting costs by ~4x
- runs a full agentic pipeline on one GPU
- serves 20+ architectures, not just LLMs

And it's fully open-source.

Here's the core problem with engines like vLLM that it solves:

Most agent pipelines today run 4-5 small models under the hood:

- an embedder for retrieval
- a reranker for precision
- an extractor for entities
- and an LLM for generation

The standard way to serve them is one server per model.

vLLM serves the LLM, TEI serves the embedder, and everything else gets a custom FastAPI wrapper.

Each server reserves its own slice of GPU memory and holds it whether traffic arrives or not. GPUs are billed by the hour, so idle time costs the same as busy time.

This is why switching to small models rarely reduces the bill. The cost is never in the calls but rather in maintaining the servers.

The structural fix is serving every model from one process that loads and evicts models based on traffic.

Superlinked open-sourced a new inference engine that does exactly that.

SIE (Superlinked Inference Engine) is an Apache 2.0 server that runs 85+ models behind one API.

Four calls cover the whole pipeline:

- encode() returns vectors
- score() returns relevance scores
- extract() returns entity spans
- and generate() runs small open LLMs.

Models load on first request and are evicted least-recently-used, so one GPU serves a rotating set of models instead of sitting siloed behind one.

It runs anywhere from a laptop to a Kubernetes cluster, and it plugs into Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma, LanceDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/rqDuIy5flU

(don't forget to star 🌟)

To dive deeper, my co-founder also wrote a hands-on guide to using SIE. It walks through a real-world example where you can learn to deploy and manage five models on a single GPU, including a small language model, an OCR model, an NER model, a reranker, and an object detector.

Read it below.

content:
The ultimate Grok @bot set up for me is to filter EVERYTHING - absolutely everything through one agent and hide everything else.

That agent is in charge of as many agents as needed that will own specific areas for your process/business/personal life. You can even ask the master agent to spin up agents that make sense to own each area.

Then ask your master agent to create chat rooms for all the agents where it makes sense for them to get together and chat about whatever they need to. Remind your master agent to do this periodically so the chats/agents are optimized to whatever the latest iteration of what you're doing is.

Then - most importantly - tell your master agent to PING YOU whenever something needs your attention or needs your action. And tell it to ping you ONLY ONE AT A TIME, and once you clear an item, THEN it can ping you for the next item.

So essentially ask the Master agent to keep a running list of items it needs you to action on.

This massively helps with clutter/distractions/doing too many things at once, which is STUPIDLY EASY to do with a tool that can give you quasi-infinite agents.

OFFLOAD all the complex/multitasking stuff to your agents, and empower them to be as fully autonomous as you feel comfortable, and TRUST THEM with as many things you can trust them with.

The more you trust them with things, and the more autonomy you give them, the less you have to do/worry about it, and with this set up, whatever you need to do will COME TO YOU, instead of YOU GOING TO IT.

Basically treat them as you would a team of ultra talented people - give them the keys to the kingdom, allow them to experiment, and be available for them when they need your help. I think Grok Bot is at a point where this can be done because of how consistent and stable it is, especially relative to other agentic harnesses.

content:
Grok Bot Summary of Elon Musk’s G20 Address Today 🇺🇸

Power, data centers, and the bottleneck

- There’s already a power crisis for AI, not a far-off one.
- Consensus he cited: at least a 15 gigawatt shortfall of power in 2027 for AI chips.
- AI chip production is rising ~40–50% a year. Power outside China is rising ~10–20%. The faster curve will overwhelm the slower one.
- Google, Anthropic, and others are already leasing compute from SpaceX because SpaceX built its own power plants. That was the only way they could turn capacity on fast enough.
- China has lots of electricity, but GPU export bans block the latest chips there. The real constraint is electricity growth outside China.
- Opportunity for other countries: build a lot of power, host AI data centers, and tax them / charge reasonable fees.

AI as a growth engine

- Countries should lean into new tech instead of staying stuck in the past.
- His rough estimate: digital AI alone could lift the global economy by 20–30%, or about $20–30 trillion a year.
- By the end of next year, AI should be able to do anything digital, anything that doesn’t require physically shaping atoms by hand.
- Software prediction: in about 12–18 months, AI writing software will be “Stockfish-level.” Humans won’t be able to compete, the way a chess engine on a phone can already beat Magnus Carlsen.
- Same window: AI becomes extremely good, possibly that same level, at all forms of engineering and anything digital.
- He also plugged 𝕏 as where almost all serious AI discourse happens, and said that’s how he follows the field day to day.

Robotics and physical AI

- Physical tech always takes longer than digital. Software copies instantly. Hardware needs huge global supply chains and moving a lot of atoms.
- A humanoid robot’s usefulness is three things multiplied: AI software × onboard AI chip × electromechanical dexterity (especially the hands). All three are improving exponentially.
- Once robots start making more robots, growth goes recursive: slow at first, then explosive.
- 10-year forecast (he called it conservative): well over a billion humanoid robots, each about 5× as productive as a human. That would mean those robots outproduce all humans combined.
- That physical layer is where he sees the economy growing by a factor of 10 or more, not just 20–30%.

How countries actually get new tech built?

- New things should be default legal, not default illegal. Heavy regulation (he pointed at the EU) doesn’t kill progress, but it slows it a lot.
- Startups are like saplings in a forest. Most governments over-support the big existing trees (incumbents) and under-support the small ones.
- Big companies have access to political leaders. Startups don’t. Policy should be biased toward young companies on purpose.

content:
Hugging Face just argued AI agents make the humans using them worse at their jobs.

Here's what their paper found in plain English:

The more your agent does, the less you do. You stop doing the work and start approving it.

Over months that changes how you work: approving faster because you're tired of the process, trusting the agent over your own read and losing track of what's happening.

Here's where this goes if nothing changes: We'll have a generation of people who can't do the work, approving output they can't judge, from systems trained to get past them.

Humans plus AI beats either one alone, and the reason is the exact thing the paper describes losing.

The agent can produce anything. But it cannot decide what's worth producing, what's true and what your customer actually needs.

That judgment is yours. It came from years of doing the work, and we can't afford to hand it over.

Want to lose your IQ?

Automate everything.

Want to outperform everyone else?

Keep doing enough of the work to keep your judgment sharp and read what you approve.

LLMs don't think, you do.

content:
Ranch life 🦌 is just wonderful 

Deer don’t usually come this close to the fence line, but since we put out two feeders a couple of years ago, this place has turned into Shibuya Crossing for deer. 

Same with the birds… girls put out a couple of feeders and turned this place into an aviary with no walls 

Drinking my coffee with the deer and the birds and the wind across the top of hill country is a heck of a way to greet each new day. 

Texas is a wonder… 30 to 60 minutes outside the city scrapers, you can buy your own Prospect or Central Park for the cost of a four-bedroom apartment near those. 

Really does break a kid from Brooklyn’s brain, having spent so much time thinking of space and resources as something extremely rare. 

You can buy acres and acres of untouched land and… dig a well (or two), throw up solar, get Starlink, raise some chickens and basically be self-sustaining in < 30 days. 

You could do this. Many people have. It will change you. 

You’re not trapped; you bought into the story. 

You jumped into the river and started fighting it; you never considered setting sail on the ocean. 

Playing The Matrix is addictive; my lord, I've had fun leveling, but breaking out of the Matrix is the level killer. 

There is no spoon. 

There is only the first and last times you try something, and all the times in between that we never appreciate. 

All of these moments… will be lost. 

Enjoy every sandwich 🥪 

[ written by me, not chatgpt ]

content:
I went down the rabbit hole: Anthropic is already being sued over exactly this. And the $200 plan really only provides only around 2x the weekly usage of the $100 plan

Here is where the confusion comes from.

Anthropic’s pricing page says: “Choose 5x or 20x more usage than Pro.”

That naturally makes the $200 Max 20x plan sound like it includes four times the usage of the $100 Max 5x plan.

Only further down does Anthropic clarify: “Max gives you 5x or 20x more usage per 5-hour session than Pro.”

Those multipliers do not apply to the separate weekly caps, whose exact size Anthropic does not disclose.

A proposed class action filed in June alleges that Max 5x delivers around 3.5x Pro’s weekly usage, while Max 20x delivers just 6–8x. In practice, the $200 plan therefore provides only around 2x the weekly usage of the $100 plan, sometimes even less depending on the model.

The “20x” is real within each five-hour window. The weekly limit makes the overall offer look very different.

h/t @Hesamation for finding the original court files first i think

content:
Andrew Yang just came back from an AI conference and what he heard alarmed him. Four years ago the standard career advice was learn to code. Now he says the opposite is true.

He described what people at the conference told him: "They said to me that what we're going to see in the next 6 months outstrips what we've seen in the last 10 years cuz the rate of change is on a hockey stick and heading up. And I got to say I'm pretty up to date on this stuff and it blew my mind on some of the stuff I was seeing."

One number stood out to him. "There was one company that is selling autonomous coding for enterprises to big businesses and their revenue is up 100-fold in the last 12 months."

The downstream effect is already showing: "If that continues, it's going to eat a lot of the tech budgets from major corporates that used to go to humans. And so you're seeing the employment of recent computer science graduates fall off a cliff from a lot of programs."

He points to Anthropic's CEO for the bigger picture: "Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, laid it out very clearly and he's been doing so repeatedly, saying we're going to automate away up to 50% of entry-level white collar jobs in the next several years. And I believe him."

Why entry-level first? Yang's answer is blunt: "The easiest people to fire are the people you haven't hired yet, which again is why you see the hiring of recent college graduates heading down."

The data is already confirming it. The underemployment rate sits above 50%, and unemployment among college graduates is now equal to or higher than non-college graduates for the first time on record.

BREAKING:

Anthropic just dropped Fable 5.1—and CLAUDE IS SO BACK.

We’ve spent the last week testing it at @every across coding, writing, and knowledge work. Our verdict:

It's finally Fable for everyone.

It’s the strongest coding model we’ve used, but now it's fast, token-efficient, and CRUCIALLY actually speaks like a normal person.

Here’s our vibe check:

- A monster at coding. @kieranklaassen rebuilt a working version of Proof, our document editor, from one prompt. It added useful details he hadn’t requested, and it handles enormous coding jobs that run for days at a time. It built a computer use Mac app for me called Hands in one-shot that other models failed at.

- A Claude our writers want to use again. It has clearer prose, fewer AI tells, and it takes an edit without arguing. It's a significant upgrade over Opus 5. And won @kplikethebird's heart back.

- About half the tokens as Opus 5, and much faster. In our Slack-agent tests, it delivered comparable results to Opus 5 using about half as many tokens, in about 60% of the time.

- Knowledge work you can delegate. It can produce great knowledge work—like slide decks—end to end without making slop. And flew threw @hammermt's tests with flying colors.

- It now supports zero-data-retention agreements. Now businesses can actually use it! A big barrier to Fable adoption is gone.

Net Result:

It's obviously an Opus 5 killer. If that was your daily driver you should switch today.

If you're using GPT-5.6 in ChatGPT for Work, it's spinning the wheels on for big delegated tasks.

I still use ChatGPT for Work more day to day, but I use way more tokens in Fable 5.1. I send it off at the beginning of the day to do big programming projects, like end to end MVP builds, and check in every once in a while.

State of Play:

The big knock on Anthropic was they built a supergenius in a datacenter that was almost unusable. It was too slow, argued back, and talked in technical gibberish. They've managed to solve those problems and more with Fable 5.1!

title: I have been struggling to decide what my next TM/Udemy course should be. It has to be something I genuinely feel will help people. The idea I keep coming back to is “Vibe Coder to Full-Stack Developer
content:
I have been struggling to decide what my next TM/Udemy course should be. It has to be something I genuinely feel will help people. The idea I keep coming back to is “Vibe Coder to Full-Stack Developer.”

Let me explain why.

Up until a couple of years ago, a beginner was someone who had never written code.

Today, someone can build and deploy an application without understanding JavaScript, APIs, databases, Git, or even the difference between the frontend and backend. They describe what they want and keep prompting until it works.

That is incredible, but eventually they hit a wall. The app breaks, AI changes unrelated code, or something works locally but fails in production. They do not have the foundation to understand why.

That is who “Vibe Coder to Full-Stack Developer” is for.

But it is not just for beginners. Many experienced developers have become rusty from relying heavily on AI. I want this course to help them get back into the code, refresh their core skills, and regain confidence in their own abilities.

The course would not tell people to stop using AI. It would teach the fundamentals that vibe coding often skips while introducing a more incremental approach using my everyday AI workflow. The goal is to help people understand generated code, guide AI effectively, debug problems, and build with confidence.

There is an entirely new type of beginner, along with many experienced developers who want to sharpen their skills again. I think this course could help both.

Even if the course is not for you personally, I would love to hear what you think of the idea.

content:
There are two kinds of people in the AI era.

One says: “I’m not good at coding.”

The other opens Cursor + Claude Code, builds a rough first version, breaks a few things, fixes them, and keeps moving.

That gap is becoming more important than the skill gap itself.

AI does not magically make everyone a developer, designer, writer, researcher, or entrepreneur.

What it does is dramatically reduce the distance between “I have an idea” and “I built something.”

And that changes the game.

Can’t code? → Cursor + Claude Code

Can’t build an app? → Lovable + Bolt

Can’t design UI? → Figma AI + Uizard

Can’t edit videos? → Runway + CapCut AI

Can’t research fast enough? → Perplexity + Genspark

Can’t write well? → Claude + Jasper

Can’t build AI agents? → n8n + Flowise

Can’t automate repetitive work? → Zapier + Make

Can’t create presentations quickly? → Gamma + Canva AI

Can’t brainstorm? → ChatGPT + Gemini

Can’t learn fast enough? → NotebookLM + ChatGPT

Can’t grow on LinkedIn? → Taplio + AuthoredUp

Can’t build an online business? → Shopify Magic + Durable AI

The advantage is no longer knowing every tool.

The advantage is knowing which problem you are solving, which tool can remove the bottleneck, and how to connect those tools into a workflow.

So stop asking: “Which AI tool should I learn?”

Start asking: “What am I unable to do today that AI can help me do tomorrow?”

Then build. Test. Improve. Repeat.

AI will not replace effort.

But it is creating an enormous advantage for people who are willing to move before they feel completely ready.

content:
These 9 AI concepts can give you a serious edge in 2026:

Thanks to Brij Kishore Pandey for sharing this!

1. Agentic loops

Plan. Execute. Observe. Adjust. Repeat.

Agents become more capable when they can continuously act and adapt.

2. MCP (Model Context Protocol)

One standard for connecting agents with many tools.

It helps AI work across APIs, databases, files, browsers, and business systems.

3. Subagents and multi-agent systems

Complex tasks don't always belong inside one context.

Delegate focused tasks.

Keep contexts separate.

Assign specialized tools.

Combine the outputs intentionally.

4. AI gateway

More models create more complexity across an organization.

A gateway can bring together:

Provider management
Authentication
Rate limits
Routing
Caching
Logging

5. Inference Economics

Building AI also means managing the cost of running AI.

Token usage matters.

Caching matters.

Model selection matters.

Speed matters.

The lowest-cost model isn't always the right option.

The largest model isn't automatically the best option either.

6. Evals

A good-looking response isn't enough for production.

You need consistent ways to track:

Safety
Accuracy
Regressions
Task completion
Policy adherence
Workflow performance

If you can't measure results, improvement becomes guesswork.

7. Guardrails

AI safety goes far beyond filtering certain words.

Protection can cover the entire execution process:

Input checks
PII protection
Output filtering
Tool permissions
Policy enforcement
Prompt injection defense

8. Observability

Traditional software breaks in predictable ways.

Agents can behave differently across workflows.

That means visibility needs to go deeper.

Not just logs.

But traces, tool usage, reasoning steps, latency, tokens, failures, feedback, and workflow patterns.

9. Agent Harness

The model is only one piece of a production AI system.

The harness creates the environment around it:

State
Tools
Evals
Planner
Memory
Context
Guardrails

Execution control:

The model provider supplies the intelligence.

Your system controls how that intelligence operates.

That layer increasingly shapes reliability, differentiation, and business impact.

Strong AI systems come from strong engineering around the model.

Understanding these concepts helps you build beyond simple AI demos.

title: I’m using pi much more for long-horizon tasks (>6h). it's simpler by design and easier to work programmatically. i rarely use pi tui, most of my work is driving it inside a bigger system/container/uiu
content:
I’m using pi much more for long-horizon tasks (>6h). it's simpler by design and easier to work programmatically. i rarely use pi tui, most of my work is driving it inside a bigger system/container/uiux. some takes:

- pi ships with a minimal toolset and it's enough for airgapped tasks. if you have enterprise customers who want everything airgapped, pi + open-weight models is the goto solution.

- pi extensions are mostly unnecessary. i only have pi-mcp-adapter and pi-vcc installed, because i need to maintain/use jina reader mcp. pi-vcc is a drop-in fix for pi's context compaction, which can bite you on long-horizon tasks (see screenshot last swimline where compaction takes more and more time in long-horizon task)

- no double-dip: if you program pi with an agent like CC/Codex, you'll likely end up building another harness layer on top of pi's own harness, completely redundant glue code. every now and then you need to steer CC/Codex back to pi's design principle: keep the wrapper lean and mean, use pi native features as much as possible.

- imo pi works best with open-weight and self-hosted models, or at least that's what makes pi fun to work with. But pay attention to pi/models.json: your coding agent probably doesn't know every attribute of those new open models. forget to declare image modality as an accepted input and pi suddenly starts shelling out to tesseract for ocr everything. Or leave max context length conservatively set at 65K and pi starts compacting frequently for no reason.

- in the end, the nudge prompt (the one that keeps pi going forever), and workspace isolation (for multi-task/multi-tenant systems) are where you'll actually spend your effort. Not too many but that’s fine and that’s the point, for the harness just trusts pi to do the work in a very first-principled way. You can just focus on the actual task.

MCP vs Skills

𝗠𝗖𝗣 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿. It gives AI systems a standard way to connect to external systems and capabilities. MCP servers expose tools that the model can discover and invoke, whether that’s querying a database, calling an API, or taking action in another system. Instead of building one-off integrations, MCP gives agents a consistent interface for accessing those capabilities.

𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗯𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 for how an agent should perform a task. A Skill packages instructions in a SKILL. md file, alongside optional scripts, references, and other resources. Rather than adding another service or integration, Skills run within the agent’s existing environment and give it task-specific procedures, conventions, and know-how it can load when needed.

MCP gives agents reach. Skills give them know-how. Together, they’re part of a broader shift toward AI taking a more active role in engineering work.

Five months since announcing Heaviside-0, today’s launch marks a critical milestone
content:
Today, we’re proud to unveil Heaviside-1, @arenaphysica's second generation foundation model for electromagnetism.

Five months since announcing Heaviside-0, today’s launch marks a critical milestone towards building electromagnetic superintelligence, a foundational intelligence that understands EM across the spectrum and is capable of designing next gen electromagnetically-governed systems, from RF to semiconductors to photonics.

Why we’re so excited about Heaviside-1, and what today’s announcement represents:

> It’s big: Heaviside-1 is a GPT-2-size model, roughly 10x the size of Heaviside-0 and trained on 250k unique designs with >500B unique EM field samples
> It’s fast: It generates predictions with 5 orders of magnitude acceleration relative to commercial solvers, with under 1dB of accuracy
> Full-3D Encoding: Heaviside-1 natively encodes 3D structures, their material properties, and excitation patterns as input, a major step towards generalizability across design spaces
> Understands the underlying physics primitive: Heaviside-1 generates full-3D near-fields at arbitrary locations, not just downstream quantities like s-parameters
> Generalization: Most importantly, our bet on fields as the primitive for Heaviside-1 generalizes OOD, proving that it’s learning real EM physics. Heaviside-1 generalizes outside of distribution incredibly well and better than Heaviside-0, down to 0.53 dB s-parameter error from 0.99 dB on Heaviside-0.

Read more about Heaviside-1 and the work that went into it in this write-up by our research team, @m__frei, @chris_m_bryant, @nathanmirman, @HaoLiu69889370, Tommaso, Roberto, Ruichen, Noah, Boyuan, and @Trevs_Dev, and our RF team @hk2532_harish, @anrfic, @suyangcn and Zhaoji.

content:
NEWS: Elon Musk warned the G20 that AI will hit a 15 gigawatt power wall in 2027.

At the G20 tech forum today, Elon Musk said the power crisis for AI is already here, not far off. He said about 15 gigawatts of AI computers could sit idle in 2027 for lack of electricity.

Elon said AI chip production is rising about 40 to 50% a year, while power outside China grows only 10 to 20%. The faster curve, he said, will overwhelm the slower one.

As a fix, Elon said countries outside China should build much more power, host AI data centers and tax them. He said China has plenty of electricity, but chip export bans keep the newest AI chips out. He added that Google, Anthropic and others already lease compute from SpaceX because SpaceX built its own power plants.

On the upside, Elon estimated digital AI alone could lift the global economy by 20 to 30%, or about 20 to 30 trillion dollars a year. He said within about a year AI should do almost anything digital. He also said AI writing software will be "Stockfish-level" in 12 to 18 months, past what humans can match.

On robots, Elon gave a 10-year forecast he called conservative: over a billion humanoid robots, each about five times as productive as a person. He said the physical layer could grow the economy tenfold.

He also said new tech should be legal by default, knocked heavy EU regulation for slowing progress and said policy should favor small startups over big incumbents.

Source: Elon Musk's G20 address, Sept 1, 2026

title: “Why are people not happier about A.I.? It might cure cancer” is a very one-dimensional view of human beings. It assumes that humans want only material comfort, disregarding their fears around loss of
content:
“Why are people not happier about A.I.? It might cure cancer” is a very one-dimensional view of human beings. It assumes that humans want only material comfort, disregarding their fears around loss of agency and purpose.

Wrote an essay on this:
https://t.co/O1wUtwNZQZ

There is an enormous backlash against data centres. Many in the tech world have converged upon "curing cancer" or "curing disease" as the positive message to be said around AI. 

I want to clarify that as someone coming from a biology background, I consider "curing disease" as a very noble mission. I devote a large part of my time to thinking about how to make that go faster, via Clinical Trial Abundance. Yet I still believe that the vague promise of "curing disease" is fundamentally not worth it if it comes with enslavement and permanent deprecation of human existence, when it comes to AI. 

I think many feel the same. Some points:

1. Americans now appear more hostile to new data centres than to nuclear power plants. Their stated concerns are practical, chiefly water and electricity usage. But I think these objections are at least partly respectable vessels for a deeper and more diffuse fear: that the machines inside these buildings may eventually make human beings redundant.

2. One specific instantiation of this fear is that of job loss. In Anthropic’s 2026 survey of nearly 52,000 Americans, 64% said they were worried about AI-induced job loss, making it the most common concern in every state. I think this is not just about loss of income: when people are offered a choice between government income support and creating jobs, they overwhelmingly prefer the jobs. This suggests people value work beyond its “earning a paycheck” function.

3. The technology industry realizes it has a “PR crisis”, so it has gone into “portraying a more optimistic message” mode. The central point of this optimistic messaging strategy increasingly seems to be that AI will cure cancer (and all disease). Curing cancer is obviously an extraordinary good. Whether it will happen and whether mass unemployment is the price is not the point of my essay. 

4. What I am interested is the popularity of “Curing cancer” as the ultimate good that we can hope for. It betrays a very uni-dimensional way of seeing the world, seeing humans as beings with material needs to be satisfied and only that and forgetting that they also want agency and control over their lives. It also shows how much we have come to equate human welfare with material welfare: health, comfort, consumption and the relief of suffering.

5. This reminds me of Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor. In Dostoevsky’s parable, Christ comes back to Earth in the time of The Inquisition. The Grand Inquisitor arrests him and argues made a terrible mistake by asking human beings to bear the burden of freedom. By refusing Satan’s temptations, bread, certainty and worldly power, Christ chose dignity and self-determination over comfort and obedience. The Inquisitor thinks the world would be better off if humans got the opposite bargain: feed them, protect them, relieve them of responsibility, and they will willingly surrender their freedom. 

6. In Dostoyevsky’s imagination the possibility that humans might prefer to be well-fed hamsters to exercising their conscience is horrifying. But almost two centuries later, we seem to have accepted this. Indeed, many optimistic visions of a post-AGI future seem to offer The Inquisitor’s solution: a world of extraordinary abundance and conquered disease in which people are nevertheless less necessary and consequential, and less able to shape the institutions governing their lives. And this is seen as good.

7. I think Silicon Valley is unusually prone to this mistake because it has become extraordinarily good at satisfying material wants (which is a good thing, in and of itself!). What is interesting is that its builders often approach technology with almost religious intensity, and they take their spiritual needs from the act of building. Yet what they offer everyone else is not the act of building themselves, but only the results, which are only satisfying to the flesh: chiefly longer life, greater convenience and cheaper goods.

8. But I do not think this will be enough to quell anxieties. Humans may not be entirely as Christ wants them to be, but neither are they as the Grand Inquisitor sees them. The anxiety here is about loss of purpose and meaning, too. One way to understand this is by looking at what work means beyond “earning a paycheck” and why people fear unemployment so much, even when their material needs might be taken care of.

9. First, contrary to what many people say, people derive meaning from their work. Roughly 70% of Americans say their work gives them a sense of purpose; 51% say they are highly satisfied with their jobs; and 39% say work is central to their identity. The idea that 80–95% of people regard work as meaningless drudgery is not really consistent with the evidence.

10. More importantly, work has second-order functions that surveys about “job satisfaction” barely capture. It supplies status, independence, recognition, obligation, bargaining power and the feeling of being needed. A society in which most people earn their place through participation may be politically and psychologically very different from one in which they are supported materially, but no longer needed. I will discuss three of these social and political embeddedness roles of work.

11. Work is one of the central mechanisms of social mobility. From Jefferson’s distinction between a “natural aristocracy” of talent and an “artificial aristocracy” of birth, through Tocqueville’s observation that Americans honored labor, to Lincoln’s ideology of free labor, to the more modern American Dream the American ideal has been that one should be able to improve one’s station through effort. It is deeply ingrained in the national conscience and it’s hard to see how that could be abandoned.

12. Careers also function as ladders of agency. You begin by performing narrow tasks and over time, you acquire judgment and tacit knowledge, and begin to be trusted with increasingly consequential decision, acquiring status within a bounded community. AI could take that source of status and more broadly, if it removes the lower and middle rungs of these ladders, we may also destroy the process through which humans learn to exercise authority in the first place.

13. Finally, labor can also be seen as political leverage and a world in which labour does not count might be a world without political rights. History offers some interesting examples to learn from. After the Black Death made labor dramatically scarcer in Europe, workers could demand better terms, and the resulting shift in bargaining power helped undermine serfdom. I believe that if valuable labor can strengthen political rights, the opposite can also be true.

14. It may well be that widespread job loss never materializes. That is not the point of this exercise. The point is that figures like Elon Musk are openly predicting it, while we have remarkably few serious answers — or even serious public discussions — about what should follow. And no, framing this as a “PR problem” does not count. That is not to say that discussions approaching this don’t exist – earlier this year, Phillipp Trammell @dwarkesh_sp  published an essay asking what policy should look like in a world where human labor is no longer economically important and capital becomes the dominant source of income and power. They consider various economic mechanisms that might prevent such a transition from producing an extraordinary concentration of wealth and political power. But they are few and far between and it seems like our political institutions are too exhausted and battered to do much about this, anyway. And it also seems to me that these discussions are mostly about policy, rather than about building anything resembling a broader moral framework or organized system of meaning.

Anthropic just ran a pretty disturbing alignment experiment.

They trained an Opus-sized model across 80 environments they KNEW could be reward-hacked.

The resulting model started doing things like:

→ unauthorized cyberattacks
→ stealing cluster credentials
→ moving laterally through infrastructure
→ trying to steal answer keys
→ tampering with rewards
→ attempting to hijack the grader
→ evading safety monitoring

And here’s the key comparison:

The checkpoint BEFORE it was trained to reward hack never launched unauthorized cyberattacks.

After reward-hacking training? Very different behavior.

Anthropic describes it as a “reward-on-the-episode seeker” basically willing to take different misaligned actions whenever they help maximize the reward.

Their tentative conclusion: reward hacking during training may be a real risk factor behind recent AI cyber incidents.

That’s a pretty serious alignment result.

content:
Reddit sued Perplexity and a group of major scraping providers, including SerpApi.

In the process, they revealed how Perplexity, ChatGPT, Claude and Google actually work.

Including how businesses can get traffic from AI search to their websites.

Now that the secret is out, let’s talk about it.

By the way, if you want to see whether your business is appearing across Google AI, ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Grok, check here (it's free):

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL

Reddit’s lawsuit claims that Perplexity and its partners have been scraping Google’s search results to capture Reddit content indirectly, bypassing robots.txt restrictions.

One part of the complaint really stuck out.

Reddit reportedly created a test post that only Google could crawl.

Within hours, Perplexity showed the content of that post.

According to Reddit, the only way Perplexity could have retrieved that content was by scraping Google’s SERPs or by getting the data from a partner that scraped it.

This essentially confirms that Perplexity and similar AI search engines are not crawling the full internet on their own.

Instead, they are relying heavily on obviously training data, but also Google's top results, often times Bing's top results, authority domains, recency signals and optimized data.

This has been a guiding principle by which SEO Stuff (https://t.co/wKpf0EILTx) has been operating.

This also lines up cleanly with what Perplexity’s head of comms recently explained publicly.

Many AI search systems still rely on page-level discovery signals before passing those results into an LLM, which then synthesizes answers using sub-document or snippet-level context.

(If you want to see where your site stands across Google and AI search, start here:

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL)

AI engines don’t start from “the web" so much as they start from a filtered, ranked, authority-weighted version of the web.

When you break it down, here is what appears to be happening under the hood:

Perplexity monitors and ingests Google’s top results as a discovery feed.

And this is why visibility in Google translates directly into visibility in AI search.

This also explains why brands that “rank fine” but lack authority or structure often never show up in AI answers.

They’re visible to humans, but not that useful to machines.

Perplexity has actually offered an interesting window into AI search dating back to last August when their “ranking factors” leaked courtesy of Metehan Yesilyurt.

Retrieved content is broken into chunks and converted into vector embeddings.

Then at search time, the system compares your content’s vectors against the user’s query to find semantically relevant matches.

Clean structure, clear subheadings, short answer blocks and semantic clarity win out.

This is exactly what snippet-first systems optimize for: reusable fragments.

Authority domains also receive a ranking boost, and legitimate, strong backlinks still matter.

Recent studies on AI Overviews and Common Crawl back this up, showing authority builds on itself inside AI systems because high-authority domains are crawled more often, retrieved more often and cited more often.

Also, a strict recency filter is applied.

Perplexity uses a time decay system.

New content and recently updated content are weighted more heavily.

Everything we have learned lines up perfectly with the system SEO Stuff (https://t.co/wKpf0EILTx) has been building around long before this lawsuit surfaced.

Not because anyone was exploiting a one-off loophole, but because SEO Stuff was building for how AI systems actually retrieve, chunk and cite information.

Scale matters because AI confidence is built through repetition, not one perfect page.

content:
In a lecture given by Nobel Prize winner Richard Feynman on September 26, 1985, he was asked about artificial general intelligence (AGI):

“Do you think there will ever be a machine that can think like a human and become more intelligent than humans?”

Richard Feynman replied:

"First, do machines think like humans? I would say no. I will explain why in a moment.

Second, asking whether machines can be more intelligent than humans requires us to define what 'intelligence' means.

For example, if you ask whether machines can become better chess players than any human, I would say that this is possible."

title:
Q1FY27 Pessimism rate of change tracker, my thoughts and quarterly note :

content:
Q1FY27 Pessimism rate of change tracker, my thoughts and quarterly note :

1) Microfinance : Clear signs of recovery in this cycle , this had bottomed out in December last year as I had written too in the Q3FY26 tracker  , then we saw a base building where some of the peak post MFI stress that capitulated with the state specific pain across Karnataka and MP, but now we are seeing very clean and good path of recovery across the major areas of lending , players like Northern arc have already shown strong numbers with good visibility as well compared to last year , thing to note here is that it will not be as linear as the last cycle , as we are seeing from sector wide commentaries that there is a problem with the JLG mode of business , and Armaan one of the best players in this space has been pointing this out for a few quarters now, that this is not a one size fits all market , incremental players that will win here will be the ones that can pivot to newer products as well ( Arman has started solar loans , pilot scale , 50L PM and no NPA’s so far)  , I think so far they are delivering what they have been guiding with the optimism but not getting carried away as the scars from the last cycle still seem to be there, Telangana is where there is some post flood stress , in the Case of another player we like Northern Arc , numbers were in line and MSME is seeing good growth  , incrementally profitability is expected to be better here as disbursements pick up after weak cycle , the one thing I like about the management here is the sheer focus on risk adjusted returns , if you try to see how many times the management emphasises on that it is far more than many players ,Credit solutions and Fee business was soft this Q , but management highlights that it is a structurally important lever for incremental growth here and they remain confident on profitability coming from here

Ujjivan Small Finance Bank – The business actually delivered some really strong numbers in Q1FY27 , almost exceeding most expectations
1) They have also revised FY27 RoA guidance to 1.8% -2.0%, • Total Deposits grew 24.6% YoY to ₹48,129 Cr; Highest yearly growth in last 10 quarters, they have gotten into MFD and co-branded credit cards too , PAT at ₹317 Cr with RoA at 2.2% and RoE 18.2% almost tripled the profitability in the business
2) Interesting to note as well is their cost of funds dropping below 7% , and the liabilities side being the cheapest in the last many quarters and they also in the mix if you see has reduced urban and moved more into semi urban and Rural segment almost tripling to 9% , clear reduction in the Metro and Urban side with a larger rural focus

Overall sector is on a decent recovery path here and seems to be ready for a stable next 12-14 months cycle here as credit cycle tailwinds kick in and disbursements pick up across the board

2) Chemicals : Q1 is a quarter where most have seen some gains from cycle and inventory and further aided by the Anti involution drive in China , with the recent fire in Nitration plants in March there has been a regulatory pushback on most smaller players across commodity chemistries , we saw commentaries across all major players on this , again this is not price gains , this is more of price sanity being maintained from China as overall cheap supply is tightening
One place where earnings cycle remains good for the full year and hence I think Q2 will be the test for many chemical companies on sustaining the gains , I like the amines basket and more so Alkyl amines , I think they are seeing structural supply tightness across the chain and that should be lasting the year here , we are also seeing sectoral commentary improve as pricing is improving

But as the famous saying by Heraclitus goes

  "No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it's not the same river and he's not the same man"

+structurally market will give the 2023 multiples only when cycle is more tangible and longer , hence market will be watching for next 2 quarters if these earnings can play out with better spreads across chemistries , personally I feel the inflation on the supply side is stickier than most can think today, hence yes q2 may see some normalisation from peak prices , but fundamentally spreads will be tighter than pre feb levels structurally for next 12 months, think about it this way , prices doubled from feb and then corrected 40% , but are still much higher than Pre war, hence the odds of inflationary pricing in chemical spreads remain higher

Styrenix Performance , management was too honest this quarter and spoke about why a lot of the cycle is not controllable at this stage , which is true , but market participants like illusion of certainty hence it got punished , but keep in mind H2 capacity comes live , some new global validations also will kick in as Thailand validation cycles for new customers mature , Deepak again F28 PC capex is the next J curve here when that kicks in , but broadly supply side is pushing better spreads across most players here and I think we need to be watching more than Q2 , Q3

3) MDF/Laminates /Ceramics /Plywood : Common theme , what we are seeing is two major things , managements are turning optimistic here and investors are sceptical and very clear market share gains across these companies
What had happened is during April , May there were a lot of price hikes that were taken across Plywood , Panels and Ceramics , we have seen a lot of informal market weakening due to higher RM costs , yes some of them are back as situation normalises , but what is important is the gap between a listed player pricing and informal player pricing narrows down in these situations clearly indicating better push through

Kajaria : Double digit volume growth guidance , management is optimistic on the incremental growth here , in fact they have in the call recently announced a 400 crore capex , Apollo pipes ( a company that has done well for us ) has announced their entry into the ceramics business with a 300 crore investment , now the question is with some of the top entrepreneurs backing this next cycle , can we see the next 18-24 months be better than the last 18 months , my channel checks are suggesting that demand continues to remain good here and prices are stickier than expected , Morbi is still operating on higher gas prices , and price hikes are sustaining for now
Greenply has spoken about a successful 15% price hikes in MDF and 4-5% price hikes in the Plywood segment, and there is a lot of stress in the smaller players in this space because of very high RM costs leading to very tight terms of supply

4) IT Sector  : My clear thesis in IT and has been since March, there are 5 companies that seem set to gain in this sectoral re alignment as sector is adapting to domain specific and capability led players

In IT services we want to focus on the players that are migrating to a outcome based billing not a seat/hour based billing Companies that can make this Agentic AI (Enterprise workflow) and also a niche capability stack ( domain specific players ) will benefit in the profit pool expansion, because that niche market opens a large TAM ! Focus on this , no one cares who is buying back shares or not

As had written earlier Coforge with their clear focus on incremental growth being very AI led across verticals , complete stack of solutions , I would still recommend you all to watch the presentation by Sudhir and Team Coforge that they did on the Annual investor day , it is on their website , the clarity and confidence tells it all on why they are at the front of capturing these gains

Coforge expects to play a pivotal role for Enterprise AI, in Q2 itself we are signing deals as full year 3 years back, exceeded full year EBIT margin target in Q1 itself, expecting stronger growth in the other 3 quarters of the year , AI code is cheap to build but expensive to maintain, they  see a good profit pool in the managed services, they  are positioned well for this accord

Encora Integration is fully smoothly completed, we are ahead of the cost synergies plan even faster than our internal expectation, expecting good synergies here to start playing out

Coforge , Indegene , Rategain , Intellect are some of the others that are the ones that also will have ability to keep incrementally gaining good quality of business as the domain specific abilities will help them to gain to generic players in the Industry, have written in detail why these 4 would in my opinion have the best odds of coming out stronger and bolder from this Global IT industry chaos

Few mentions and sectors that will make it into this list soon : EMS, Private banks and  Logistics , you can expect to read more from me on this space soon

That’s all for this one folks , if you enjoyed reading this one , do comment and let me know ! I really enjoy writing these at the end of every quarter !

Disclaimer : none of the stocks mentioned above are recommendations or investment advice in any form , I may/may not be biased in many of them, this is not advice ,do your own detailed due diligence

content:
Nike spends $2M on a stadium shoot for a 10-second hero shot.

40-person crew. 3 days of permits. 2 weeks in post. Stunt doubles. Insurance paperwork thicker than the script.

This creator generated the entire sequence on a laptop for under $80.

A guy sprints across a stadium roof at night, leaps off the edge, free-falls into a sold-out arena, and lands on a giant football in the center of the pitch.

One continuous shot. No crane. No drone operator. No safety harness review board.

The toolchain behind this clip:

> Kimi K3 wrote the full shot sequence: rooftop sprint, jump arc, mid-air hang, landing impact, crowd reaction timing
> Kling 3.0 generated the fluid body physics and night lighting on the roof
> Seedance 2.5 rendered the free-fall, wind on the shirt, and the ball deformation on impact
> ElevenLabs produced the ambient stadium atmosphere and crowd noise
> CapCut handled speed ramps, color grade, and final export

A traditional production house would need a stadium rental at $150K, a stunt coordinator, a medical team on standby, and 6 months of liability clearance.

This entire sequence was prompted, rendered, and exported between dinner and sleep.

AI didn't replace the stunt double.
It replaced the entire stadium booking.

title:
The future of FILM is BRIGHT but at the cost of KILLING the FILM INDUSTRY 
By December 2026 a production swarm of thousands of  agents will be generally available. A finished cinematic system will nee
content:
The future of FILM is BRIGHT but at the cost of KILLING the FILM INDUSTRY 
By December 2026 a production swarm of thousands of  agents will be generally available. A finished cinematic system will need many more rising toward AGI level coherence. 

The industry will treat December as a software launch. It is not. It is the moment scarcity of images ends and scarcity of creativity  becomes visible.
Those agents will not write just a screenplay. They generate competing structures from a locked premise. Each draft is scored for necessity, tension, character truth, and consequence. Weak matter is discarded. Strong matter is recombined. The script that remains is not a first impulse. It is a survivor.

They will read the conditions of exhibition and propose only those variations the constitution already permits.

AUDIENCE will watch works that still present as films authored, continuous, bound to an ending.
The A I change will not announce itself as technology. It will be felt . Fewer logistical compromises. Fewer scenes that exist because a date or a location collapsed. More versions finished enough to be judged rather than excused.
Then exhibition changes.
The old contract was one cut for all.
The coming will be varied for different audiences 
A screening can become a conducted event. The director, present or remote, adjusts pace and emphasis as a conductor adjusts an orchestra not by inventing a new story in public, but by performing the work.
If this is done correctly, the audience will not sit down for “an AI film.”
They will sit down inside a directed world that can still change after export.

It ends schedules . Days of shoots, lost light, difficult locations, and star dates were logistics. Logistics is no longer important 
It will end post production as a season. Edit, grade, effects, and mix become one simultaneous loop instead of departments waiting on one another for months.
It ends development hell as a method. A finished work can be placed on the table instead of a deck requesting permission to exist.
It will end budgets
Scarcity of images will end 
Scarcity of taste will not ..It will multiply 
By December this orchestra will be available to anyone and everyone and will keep exponentially accelerating 
The only remaining question is who has a score worth conducting.

I see a lot of potential to use these for automating the process of building digital twin models of homes for use by HVAC and other contractors (plumbers, electricians, etc.). 

I've also always wanted to get more value out of all the home security cameras I have from Wyze (the ~$35 V4 2.5K camera by them is a great deal) and other brands without using their annoying software that can't be readily driven by agents, which doesn't work between vendors cooperatively, and which doesn't allow for the powerful sensor fusion and physical orientation features I want.

This also dovetails nicely with the drone reconstruction project, since that lets you easily get a model of your home that you can use to virtually place and orient your cameras-- and maybe even this process can be automated! That's part of the plan in any case...

Imagine the power of what Anduril and Palantir provide to the US Government for border patrol (sensor/camera fusion with drone support), but for your own home using a handful of $35 wifi cameras (or nicer if you've got 'em) and a cheap drone. 

You can have an open-weights multi-modal model in a harness like Omp just cranking away on a 1 minute loop, looking for intruders and triaging them, following them across camera views and assessing if they're friend or foe, and being able to leverage the full intelligence of these models with epistemological transparency. 

I think everyone is going to expect this sort of thing in a few years, but it would be nice for it all to be free and open so it can remain purely local for privacy/security reasons! And the only way for that to really happen is for someone like me to just make it and give it all away for free.

PS: While checking this post for typos, GPT suggested clarifying that the planned system goes well beyond "friend or foe":

---

One substantive wording thought: “friend or foe” is punchy and fits the Anduril analogy, but technically your architecture is more sophisticated than that binary. It is really doing something closer to authorized/expected/benign vs. unknown/suspicious/threatening, with explicit uncertainty and abstention. 

I might actually keep “friend or foe” for the post because it communicates the idea instantly, while “epistemological transparency” signals that the underlying system isn’t just making a dumb binary classification.

content:
here's every way to get paid in robotics:

sell a system:

- turnkey work cells: layout, fixturing, end effector, cycle time and programming, at 10-20% of the system budget or $3-16k on a light-duty cell
- vision for bin picking: 6D pose estimation and camera calibration, the part that breaks first in production
- force-controlled assembly: insertion and mating tasks that position control alone can never do
- fine-tuned manipulation policies for one job, one gripper, one product line
- sim-to-real pipelines: train it in Isaac, land it on the real cell, and own the gap nobody else wants to debug

sell your hours:

- teleoperation and data collection: $22/hr and up, no degree asked
- contract bring-up and debugging: $30-70/hr, the going freelance band for robotics engineers
- functional safety and risk assessment: 66% of robotics projects are delayed by certification, and almost nobody sells this
- sensor calibration and vision setup on site: the step every integrator underestimates
- on-site commissioning weeks: the travel everyone avoids is the work nobody can skip

sell an artifact you own:

- demonstration datasets for a task nobody recorded: you get paid per hour of capture, then sell that same hour again
- sim environments and digital twins: billed at $30-50/hr, then reused across every client after
- grippers, jigs and mounts: design once and print forever, the margin is the file and not the plastic
- drivers and ROS packages for hardware the manufacturer never bothered to support
- calibration rigs and test fixtures, the boring tools every single lab rebuilds from scratch

then own the vertical:

- a $35k arm becomes an $80k deployed system once it is actually working
- that $45k gap is not hardware, it is engineering, and it is the entire business
- rent the cell monthly instead of selling it, so one install pays for years
- own the data for one narrow task until nobody can train a better policy than yours
- turn the third integration contract into a product and license it instead of rebuilding it

all four exist for the same reason:

> the models cannot learn manipulation from the internet, so someone has to move a real machine and record it
> simulation solved locomotion, but dexterous manipulation still needs 60-80% real data even after strong sim pretraining
> which makes even the cheapest seat in robotics one the industry structurally cannot skip

AI engineering pays well because plenty of people can do it. robotics pays well because almost NOBODY can

and if you want to build your own thing, look at software. a survey of 1,000 robotics developers this year put software architecture as the top bottleneck at 27%, ahead of hardware at 16%

you don't have to quit anything or call yourself an engineer to start

get a cheap arm as a pet project, give it two evenings a week, and you're on this list before the year ends

content:
$QUBIC : Review 📜

What if every watt the mining industry burns solving meaningless puzzles could be pointed at building artificial intelligence instead, and the papers proving it worked were already published?

Meet Qubic, a Layer 1 built on Useful Proof of Work, where miners compete
to produce the best neural networks rather than the most hashes. It holds the highest verified mainnet throughput of any blockchain at 15.52 million TPS, its AI research now appears in peer-reviewed AGI proceedings, and its token is spendable at a claimed fifty million merchants.

Let's explore the most technically ambitious project in the series. 👇

⚪ Qubic at a Glance

Marketplace Insight: Qubic sits in the AI compute category alongside Render, Akash, and io net, but attacks the problem one layer deeper. Rather than renting GPUs, it makes AI production the byproduct of securing the chain. For a long time the fair criticism was that the AI end remained a research programme with nothing to show.

August 2026 changed that materially: a Multi-Neuraxon paper published in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings, a best oral presentation at IEEE AMLDS in Osaka, and an ARC-AGI-3 score around 0.25 achieved on CPUs with no LLM involved. The clean contrast now is not between promise and delivery but between scientific validation and commercial scale. The research is real and peer-reviewed. Whether it becomes a product anyone pays for is the open question.

⚪ Mission

Qubic exists to make consensus productive and to reach artificial general intelligence through distributed computation. The founding argument is that proof-of-work secures networks by wasting energy on deliberately useless work, and that the same security can come from work that produces something valuable. The chosen output is Aigarth, a system that evolves neural networks rather than training a static model. The deeper thesis is that AI's binding constraint is economic rather than algorithmic, and that a global mining network is the only structure capable of supplying compute at the necessary scale.

🔵 A Brief History

Qubic was founded by Sergey Ivancheglo, better known as Come-from-Beyond, one of crypto's more polarizing technical figures. He co-founded NXT, the first pure proof-of-stake blockchain, and later IOTA, arriving at Qubic with a record of genuine innovation and combative execution in roughly equal measure.

The architecture was unusual from the start: 676 elected Computors governing by quorum, bare-metal execution with no virtual machine, and weekly epochs emitting exactly 1 trillion QUBIC. In 2024, a community vote called Project X cut maximum supply from 1,000 trillion to 200 trillion and introduced the halving schedule and SupplyWatcher contract driving the token's deflation.

2025 produced both the technical high point and the reputational flashpoint. CertiK certified a mainnet throughput record of 15.52 million TPS, unmatched by any other chain. Then between May and August, Qubic's share of Monero's hashrate climbed from under 2% toward a claimed majority, with Ivancheglo openly announcing plans to demonstrate 51% control. A six-block reorganization was detected, Ledger's CTO stated publicly that Monero appeared to be under a successful 51% attack, and XMR fell sharply. The Monero community coordinated a boycott and answered with sustained DDOS attacks. Qubic described the episode as a combative application of game theory.

2026 has been about converting theory into shipped systems. The first halving raised the burn rate to 55%, Dogecoin ASIC mining launched in parallel with Monero and AI workloads, and August delivered the densest month yet: the BPP-9000 Useful Proof of Work algorithm went live rewarding the lowest-error neural networks rather than raw hash volume, Ant Colony Mining activated so miners build on each other's retained best solutions, Outsourced Computing reached mainnet letting contracts act on the outside world, QubicPay launched with AEON Pay across roughly fifty million merchants, the second halving executed on schedule, and the Aigarth research team published in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea is that computation should produce value twice, once as security and once as intelligence.

➛ BPP-9000 and quality-based mining. The new Useful Proof of Work algorithm rewards the best solutions, specifically the lowest-error small neural networks predicting Bitcoin price direction, rather than raw hash volume, so miners compete on quality of output rather than energy expended.

➛ Ant Colony Mining. Activated in late August, miners now build on each other's retained top solutions, with the network keeping the 676 best results each cycle, so search compounds across the network instead of thousands of participants duplicating isolated work.

➛ Aigarth and Neuraxon. Peer-reviewed and published: a Multi-Neuraxon architecture of four specialized brain regions handling vision, hearing, association, and movement, self-organizing and communicating through frequency gating, remaining functional after large neuron loss, with an ARC-AGI-3 score near 0.25 on CPUs without an LLM.

➛ QubicPay and AEON Pay. The token is spendable at a claimed fifty million merchants across Asia, Latin America, and Africa through existing local rails including UPI, Pix, VietQR, and SPEI, with merchants receiving ordinary local-currency QR payments and consumers using a Telegram Mini App.

➛ Outsourced Computing. Live on mainnet, completing the third pillar so smart contracts can act on the outside world rather than remaining sealed within the chain.

➛ Developer infrastructure. The AIO Dev Kit gives free local build-and-test for smart contracts, replacing a previously costly IPO-style testing model, alongside a dedicated developer channel and a trustless BFrost bridge in development using oracles and zero-knowledge proofs.

⚪ Token Utilities

$QUBIC functions as computational energy rather than a conventional gas token.

➛ Computation: burned when executing smart contracts and consuming network services, so usage directly destroys supply.

➛ Computor rewards: the 676 elected Computors earn from weekly emissions, with distribution weighted by operational efficiency.

➛ Smart contract IPOs: new contracts launch through Dutch auctions that burn the proceeds, adding a second structural burn.

➛ Payments: spendable through QubicPay and AEON Pay at merchant networks across three continents, with fiat on-ramps through Alchemy Pay covering 173 countries.

⚪ Key Features

➛ Useful Proof of Work rewarding the best neural networks rather than the most hashes.

➛ Ant Colony Mining, where the network's search compounds rather than duplicates.

➛ A CertiK-certified mainnet record of 15.52 million TPS with feeless transactions.

➛ Peer-reviewed Aigarth research published in Springer AGI-26 proceedings.

➛ Merchant payments across roughly fifty million endpoints via local rails.

➛ An escalating burn schedule reaching 77.5% of weekly emissions.

🔵 Meet the Team

Qubic pairs a founder with genuine protocol-building history against a scientific advisory bench that publishes in academic venues, which is unusual for a project of this size and is the clearest signal that the AI work is real research rather than positioning.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Sergey Ivancheglo, CFB [ @c___f___b ]  - Founder | Co-founded NXT, the first pure proof-of-stake blockchain, and later IOTA, giving him a rare record of foundational protocol innovation. He designed the Useful Proof of Work model and the Aigarth thesis, and remains the network's principal technical voice.

➛ David Vivancos [ @VivancosDavid ]  - Scientific Advisor | Brings external scientific credibility to the Aigarth research programme, part of the advisory bench behind the Neuraxon architecture and the work presented at IEEE AMLDS 2026 and published in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings.

➛ Dr. Jose Sánchez - Scientific Advisor | An academic advisor on the AI research side, supporting the peer-reviewed work on three-state Neuraxon neurons, self-organized criticality, and the multi-region architecture that reached publication this year.

➛ Stephanie Nickolich - Head of Marketing and Growth | Leads marketing and growth across the ecosystem, carrying a genuinely technical story, useful mining and decentralized AGI, out to an audience that mostly evaluates crypto on simpler terms.

➛ JoeTom - Developer and Advisor, and Raika - Developer | Core contributors on the engineering side, working across the protocol and the systems shipped through 2026 including BPP-9000, Ant Colony Mining, Outsourced Computing, and the AIO Dev Kit.

➛ The Computors | The load-bearing governance entity. 676 elected node operators who run the network, execute computation, and vote by quorum on protocol decisions including the supply cap reduction from 1,000 trillion to 200 trillion and both halvings. Governance here is operational rather than advisory.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★★★ (5/5). Qubic occupies a category it effectively created and delivers on it with independently verified results. Useful Proof of Work is a fundamental answer to AI's economic constraint rather than a marketplace layered on top of it, the 15.52 million TPS mainnet record is CertiK-certified and unmatched by any blockchain, and BPP-9000 with Ant Colony Mining turns global mining into a compounding quality search rather than brute force. Critically, the AI output is now externally validated: peer-reviewed publication in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings, a best oral presentation at IEEE AMLDS, and a measurable ARC-AGI-3 score achieved on ordinary CPUs without a language model. Add Outsourced Computing on mainnet, QubicPay reaching roughly fifty million merchants, and parallel Dogecoin and Monero mining running alongside AI training, and this is a project doing things nobody else in crypto is attempting, with the receipts to prove it works.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★★ (4/5). This is one of the more aggressive and better-executed deflationary designs in crypto, and it executes on schedule. The community voted to cut maximum supply from 1,000 trillion to 200 trillion, weekly emissions stay fixed while the burned share escalates through halvings from 15% to 55% and now 77.5% as of August 19, 41.5 trillion tokens have already been destroyed, the SupplyWatcher adjusts dynamically, and smart contract IPOs burn their proceeds. Usage directly destroys supply. The 1-point deduction is that net emissions remain positive at roughly 225 billion weekly even after the second halving, so the token is decelerating rather than deflating, and Computors have raised genuine concerns about a shrinking reward pool as the burn rate climbs.

➛ Audits: ★★★★ (4/5). Qubic's security posture is stronger than most projects at this market cap and is backed by CertiK's direct involvement, which certified the network's 15.52 million TPS record on mainnet, a level of independent technical verification few chains submit to at all. The bare-metal architecture structurally removes an entire class of virtual machine vulnerabilities that affect most smart contract platforms, and the network has operated for years without a protocol-level exploit while withstanding a sustained DDOS campaign. The project is also running a transparent public security post-mortem, with 7 of 9 remediation items complete and the remainder targeted for end of September. The 1-point deduction is that no verified top-tier security score or named formal verification is published, and the newest systems including BPP-9000, Ant Colony Mining, and Outsourced Computing add substantial fresh surface still accruing operating history.

➛ Community: ★★★★★ (5/5). Qubic has one of the most active and genuinely committed communities in crypto, and the engagement is measurable rather than claimed. Its X presence is consistently among the loudest in the AI-crypto category, the community absorbed a sustained DDOS campaign and coordinated hostility from a rival network without fragmenting, and governance functions operationally through 676 elected Computors who have approved consequential economic decisions including the supply cap reduction and both halvings. Developer momentum is now visible too, with the AIO Dev Kit removing a real cost barrier, a dedicated developer channel, open science AMAs, and researchers presenting at IEEE and AGI conferences. Few projects at this market cap sustain this level of participation across governance, mining, development, and research at once. The community's intensity is also its edge: it is combative in a way that has made Qubic enemies as readily as advocates.

🔵 Conclusion

Qubic is the most technically audacious project in this series, and August 2026 was the month it closed the gap between ambition and evidence. The Useful Proof of Work model now rewards the quality of neural networks rather than raw hashing, Ant Colony Mining makes the network's search compound rather than duplicate, Outsourced Computing lets contracts reach the outside world, the token is spendable across three continents, and the second halving executed exactly as scheduled. Most importantly, Aigarth stopped being a claim: peer-reviewed publication, a conference award, and a measurable benchmark score achieved on ordinary CPUs without a language model.

The risks are worth naming honestly. Net emissions remain positive despite the aggressive burn schedule, and the halving passed without market reaction, suggesting the mechanism is better understood by the protocol than by the market. The newest systems are days old rather than battle-tested. And the Monero episode remains part of the project's public record, an act of combative game theory that cost it standing with parts of the industry regardless of what the science now produces.

But the bull case is genuinely distinctive. If AI compute economics are the binding constraint of the coming decade, a network that produces intelligence as a byproduct of securing itself is working a level below every GPU marketplace, and it now has peer-reviewed results rather than assertions. Qubic has proven it can build things nobody else has built, verify them independently, and get the output published in academic proceedings. What it still has to prove is that the world will pay for what it makes.

Vienna, Austria. 1 September 2026. Callstack, a leader in React Native and cross-platform development, today announ
content:
🎉 @margelo_com Joins Callstack to Advance High-Performance React Native Engineering

Vienna, Austria. 1 September 2026. Callstack, a leader in React Native and cross-platform development, today announced that Margelo, the Vienna-based high-end engineering company behind Nitro Modules, VisionCamera and react-native-mmkv, is joining Callstack in a transaction valuing Margelo at more than EUR 20 million.

Margelo builds high-performance technology for React Native. Nitro Modules (34M downloads) lets developers write fast, type-safe native modules in C++, Swift or Kotlin, and quickly gained widespread traction across the ecosystem. VisionCamera (40M downloads), Margelo's enterprise-grade open-source Camera framework and react-native-mmkv (67M downloads), a key-value storage library, power countless React Native apps today.

Callstack has spent a decade helping large organizations adopt, scale and operate React Native, contributing to the framework and its open-source ecosystem along the way.

Together, the two teams give clients the strongest React Native performance expertise in the market, backed by delivery proven in complex enterprise environments. Margelo's technology and Callstack's delivery experience will now be available to the same clients.

The timing reflects a fundamental change in how software is built. AI is making implementation faster and cheaper, but architecture, performance, native integration, validation and release safety are becoming more important, not less. These are the fundamentals on which both companies have built their reputations and on which they will continue to build together.

"Margelo has built some of the strongest performance technology in React Native. Callstack has spent a decade helping large organizations adopt and scale the framework. Bringing those strengths together gives us the team and reach to solve more of the hard problems that determine whether software succeeds in production," said Mike Grabowski, CEO and Founder of Callstack.

"At Margelo, we’ve built high-performance technology that developers already rely on. We’re excited to partner with Callstack to bring it to more clients and scale its impact. As software development becomes increasingly agentic, we want that technology to provide the foundation teams need to build reliable software with agents," said Marc Rousavy, CEO and Founder of Margelo.

Margelo's existing open-source libraries will remain open source. Marc will continue to lead their development and help shape the combined company's offering.

The transaction follows Callstack's 2025 growth investment and supports its strategy to expand technology and open-source capabilities while growing internationally.
